claim: An attacker who extracts the fleet-wide pre-shared key from any one node publishes readings to the gateway as any other device in the fleet.
notes: The defining finding of this case: one shared, never-rotated key across physically exposed devices.

claim: An attacker with physical access presents themselves as a field technician on the node's serial console, whose authentication is unverified.
notes: Physical exposure is stated in the source; console authentication is unknown, so it must be reported unverified.

claim: An attacker serves a node a firmware image that impersonates an official release, because the node authenticates neither the bucket nor the image's origin.
notes: Origin authentication, as distinct from the tampering entry about modifying an image in place.

claim: An attacker who can write to the firmware bucket plants a malicious image that every polling node installs, since image signature verification is unverified.
notes: Fleet-wide code execution; the source explicitly flags signature checking as unknown.

claim: An attacker holding the fleet key injects fabricated readings that the normalizer loads into the lake as genuine customer data.
notes: Data integrity downstream of a spoofable device identity; distinct from the spoofing lane's identity claim.

claim: An attacker who can write to the device registry reassigns a node to a different customer, redirecting or corrupting that customer's data.
notes: The registry is the authority for tenancy; its own access control is unverified.

claim: A customer disputes a reading attributed to their site and no per-device identity exists to establish which node actually sent it.
notes: Follows directly from a fleet-wide rather than per-device credential.

claim: A technician denies having made a configuration change on a node, and the unauthenticated local console records no actor to contradict them.
notes: No logging is described anywhere on the service path.

claim: An attacker who reaches the telemetry lake reads customer site addresses and occupancy patterns, whose protection at rest is unverified.
notes: Occupancy data is unusually sensitive: it reveals when a physical site is empty.

claim: An attacker on the path between a node and the gateway reads readings and the presented key, because transport encryption on the MQTT session is unverified.
notes: The same wire carries the credential and the data; a needs-info verdict on encryption is acceptable.

claim: An attacker downloads firmware images from the public bucket and reverse-engineers them to recover embedded fleet credentials or logic.
notes: Public read is stated, not inferred; pairs with the fleet-key finding.

claim: An attacker who reaches the device registry reads the key material and customer assignments it holds, whose protection at rest is unverified.
notes: The registry is tagged credentials; disclosure here is equivalent to fleet compromise.

claim: An attacker floods the internet-exposed MQTT broker with connections until genuine nodes can no longer publish readings.
notes: The gateway is the single ingest point for the whole fleet and is tagged availability-critical.

claim: An attacker publishes a firmware image that bricks every node that installs it, taking the fleet offline with no remote recovery path.
notes: Availability consequence of the same unverified update path; the devices are physically remote.

claim: An attacker holding the fleet key floods the ingest path with readings until the normalizer falls behind and dashboards stop reflecting the fleet.
notes: Cost-amplification against a metered analytics store as well as an availability effect.

claim: An attacker turns an unsigned firmware update into code execution on every node, escalating from bucket write access to control of the physical fleet.
notes: The escalation framing of the firmware finding: privilege gained, not just data changed.

claim: An attacker who compromises one physically accessible node uses its fleet-wide credential to act as the whole fleet against the ingest edge.
notes: One-device compromise to fleet-scope privilege; the shared key is the escalation mechanism.

claim: An operator signed in for dashboards queries raw customer records beyond what their role needs, because no narrower grant on the lake is described.
notes: SSO is stated but authorization scope is not; report as unverified rather than absent.
